sections.h2: Bridgeport and who handles the tax
sections.html:
Bridgeport is Connecticut's most populous city, with 148,654 residents in 2020. It sits in eastern Fairfield County where the Pequonnock River reaches Long Island Sound, about 60 miles from Manhattan. Two city offices divide the property tax job. The Tax Assessor sets values, and the Tax Collector sends bills and takes payments.

Bridgeport became a town in 1821 and a city in 1836. Of its 19.4 square miles, 16.0 are land. The city stands only 3.3 feet above sea level, which explains why buyers ask about flooding and storms. Bridgeport grew up as a port and factory town, so housing age and condition swing widely between neighborhoods.

Multiply the property's assessed value by the mill rate and you have the bill. A mill is $1 of tax on every $1,000 of assessment. The city's rates for fiscal year 2026-2027 are 27.95 mills for real estate and personal property and 31.75 mills for motor vehicles.

The city describes assessed value as 70 percent of market value, which is why the number on your notice looks smaller than a sale price. Read the bill against that assessed figure, and leave neighbors' sale prices out of it. The Tax Collector's general tax information page posts the mill rate history, and the Tax Assessor's page explains how taxes are determined.

Assessment happens as of October 1. The tax is levied the following July 1 and collected in two installments. State law treats an installment as delinquent once the first day of the next month arrives without payment.

InstallmentDueDelinquent if unpaid after
FirstJuly 1August 1
SecondJanuary 1February 1

June 30, the final day of the fiscal year, is when the city files liens. The collector can tell you whether one was filed on your property.

sections.h2: Interest and how payments are applied
sections.html:
Section 12-146 of the Connecticut General Statutes puts interest on the overdue part of a tax at 18 percent a year, counted from the original due date. A partial month counts as a full one. There is a $2 minimum per installment unless the municipality voted against it, and interest continues even after a judgment for the city.

Partial payments go first to interest and then to principal. Timeliness is judged by the municipal electronic payment service's timestamp or by the postmark on the envelope.

sections.h2: How to appeal your Bridgeport assessment
sections.html:
Take an assessment dispute to the Board of Assessment Appeals, in writing, by February 20 at the latest. The statute allows paper or email, in whatever way the board prescribes, and the Tax Assessor's office can hand you the current year's form. Your filing has to carry these items:

  • Who owns the property, and who is signing and in what position.
  • What the property is.
  • A contact name, mailing address and email address for every letter the board sends.
  • Why you are appealing and what you think the value is.
  • A dated signature from the owner or an authorized agent.

Each filer hears about the hearing's date, time and place by March 1, with at least seven calendar days of warning. A commercial, industrial, utility or apartment property assessed above $1 million may be denied a hearing, in which case the owner can head straight to Superior Court under section 12-117a.

An extension granted to the assessor pushes the filing deadline to March 20 and moves hearings into April. When the board changes a gross assessment, the new number holds until the next revaluation, apart from narrow exceptions for new construction, damage, demolition, court orders and factual corrections.

Someone who took title after the assessment date may appeal too, as may a lessee whose recorded lease obliges them to pay the real property taxes.

sections.h2: Flood zone questions for a coastal house
sections.html: A shoreline city fields storm and flood questions that towns inland rarely hear. Hurricanes and tropical storms struck the Connecticut coast in 1903, 1938, 1944, 1954, 1960 and 1985, and again with Hurricane Sandy in 2012. Expect a buyer, an insurer or a lender to ask whether the house is in a flood zone, and expect extra scrutiny of older basements, roofs and sea walls. Pull together flood insurance papers and repair records before listing.

sections.h2: Selling with unpaid Bridgeport property tax
sections.html:
Ask the Tax Collector for a payoff figure ahead of closing, since a delinquent balance keeps growing at 18 percent a year. The closing agent can settle the tax from sale proceeds if the figure matches the closing date.

  • Write down which installments are open, July, January or both, and the fiscal year of each.
  • Find out the interest so far and how much more accrues each month if the closing is delayed.
  • Ask whether a lien went on file last June 30.
  • If you think the assessment is too high, February 20 is a hard stop. Act before a closing is on the calendar.

sections.h2: What a cash sale does with an unpaid bill
sections.html:
A bill in arrears does not rule out a cash sale. The buyer takes the house as is, the title company requests the payoff figure, and what is owed comes out of the proceeds at closing. No bank is involved, so no bank appraisal has to be satisfied. Bring your notices, any lien paperwork and the mortgage servicer's details to the first conversation.

Three questions will come from the title company. Which installments are still open? Is a lien on file? Does anyone besides the owner of record have a right to sign? Settle them early. Each month a closing slips adds interest to a delinquent bill, so a clean file saves real money.

One more habit pays off: keep the paper trail. Save every notice, every receipt and any email from the collector. If the amount a closing agent quotes differs from your records, the file lets you ask a specific question and get a specific answer, and that is much faster than arguing from memory.

sections.h2: What should a seller do before listing?
sections.html:
Think in terms of the tax calendar. If it is spring and you believe the assessment is off, the filing window closes on February 20, so appeal before you sign a listing agreement. If a July or January installment is open, pay it or ask the collector for the exact amount including interest, so the buyer's attorney sees a clean record.

Next, ask the Tax Collector whether a lien was filed on the last June 30, and ask the Tax Assessor's office for the current year's application form if you plan to appeal. Finally, check your flood status and collect insurance papers. A seller who arrives with these items already settled usually negotiates from a stronger position, and a closing agent can finish the tax line without delay.

faqs.q: What is the Bridgeport mill rate?
faqs.a: The city's 2026-2027 figures are 27.95 mills for real estate and personal property and 31.75 mills for vehicles. A mill equals $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessment.

faqs.q: When are Bridgeport property taxes due?
faqs.a: July 1 and January 1. An installment turns delinquent if it goes unpaid past the first day of the following month.

faqs.q: What interest does Bridgeport charge on late tax?
faqs.a: Section 12-146 sets 18 percent a year on the overdue portion, with a $2 minimum per installment unless the city votes otherwise. A partial month counts in full.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Bridgeport assessment?
faqs.a: February 20 for the written appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals, or March 20 if the assessor received an extension.

faqs.q: Can a new owner appeal an assessment from before the purchase?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 12-111 allows anyone who received title after the assessment date to appeal to the board.
